source: Taatgen & Lee (2003) Production compilation: a simple mechanism to model complex skill acquisition (Human Factors)
finding: Production compilation merges task-independent rules plus declarative task instructions into fast task-specific rules. An ACT-R model with all default parameters learned a simulated air traffic control task this way.
numbers: Compared to Ackerman & Kanfer (1994) Study 2: 65 undergraduates, 18 trials of 10 min, model compared on trials 1-10. Planes landed per trial r2=.97; land unit task r2=.98; queue unit task r2=.91; keystroke level r2=.87. Model 5 runs x 10 trials.
quote: consists of combining and specializing task-independent procedures into task-specific procedures
limits: Model starts with too much knowledge, so it beats people on trial 1. It is slower than people on move and queue unit tasks. It has no use of cognitive slack time and no strategy discovery, so it misses individual differences.
agent_relevance: The human template for our lesson-to-routine step: instructions are first used as slow declarative text, then specialised into a fast rule. Our agent must also start from stated knowledge, and the early model-vs-human gap shows compilation is not the whole story.

source: Taatgen & Lee (2003), limitations section
finding: The authors state that compilation from experience (learning from errors) was not explored in this model. An earlier ACT-R model (Taatgen 2002) did remember illegal weather-plane-runway combinations and compile them into avoidance rules.
numbers: Not quantitative. Fit for the keystroke level (r2=.87) is lowest of the three levels.
limits: Single task, single model, one data set (Ackerman 1988 as reported). Fit at lower levels depends on the modelers' strategy choice (check landing before moving).
agent_relevance: Compiling failures into avoid-rules is the closest human analogue to storing a lesson from a failed attempt. Our G2 (revise only from real output) matches: the rule is made from an observed failure.

source: Wray, Kirk & Laird (2025) Applying Cognitive Design Patterns to General LLM Agents
finding: Names 'knowledge compilation' as a design pattern for LLM agents: cache the result of costly reasoning as a compact form for reuse. Cites ACT-R production compilation and Soar chunking as the origin. Says direct online caching of LLM reasoning in natural language is not yet widely researched.
numbers: No experiments. Lists examples: Voyager (JavaScript skills), LLMRG graphs, Reflexion reflection memory, ExpeL (as 'knowledge compilation NL'), Zhu & Reid (Soar productions from LLM reasoning).
quote: direct, online caching of LLM responses in natural language has not yet become widely researched
limits: Position paper; no measured results. Mapping of ExpeL and Reflexion to compilation is the authors' framing.
agent_relevance: Confirms the slot in our schema: lesson to routine is the knowledge-compilation pattern. Gives a list of systems to test against.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan & Griffiths (2023/2024) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: Frames language agents as production systems. Notes Soar can write new productions into procedural memory (chunking). Warns that for language agents, writing to procedural memory is much riskier than writing to episodic or semantic memory.
numbers: No experiments.
quote: significantly riskier than writing to episodic or semantic memory, as it can easily introduce bugs
limits: Conceptual framework. Does not mention ACT-R production compilation by name in the passages read; mentions Soar learning.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a gate on any new routine: a compiled routine must pass a check before it enters procedural memory (G3). Lessons stay as text; routines need verification.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with LLMs
finding: GPT-4 agent stores each verified successful program in a skill library, retrieved by embedding of its description; later skills call earlier ones. This is routine-building from success, with an environment check before commit.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distances, tech-tree milestones up to 15.3x faster (wooden 15.3x, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x) than prior SOTA; only method to reach diamond tool (1/3 runs, 102 iterations). 3 runs per method.
limits: Minecraft only; GPT-4 only; 3 seeds. Counted in prompting iterations, not wall time. Commit is gated by self-verification module plus environment feedback.
agent_relevance: Best-known LLM analogue of compilation. Gate = verified success before storing. Library is retrieved, not fired automatically, so there is no true 'rule firing without the model'.

source: Voyager ablation (Table 2, Section 3.4)
finding: Removing the skill library hurts later stages most. Without it the agent matches early tool levels but plateaus.
numbers: Iterations to unlock tool (mean+-sd, successes/3): iron 29+-11 (3/3) without library vs 21+-7 (3/3) with; diamond not reached (0/3) without vs 102 (1/3) with. Wooden 7+-2 vs 6+-2; stone 9+-4 vs 11+-2 (no gain early).
quote: exhibits a tendency to plateau in the later stages
limits: Tiny N (3 runs). Early-stage times show no benefit or slightly worse, so gain appears only when skills build on skills.
agent_relevance: Compilation pays off through composition (skills built on skills), as in ACT-R, not through single reuse. Test our routines on chained tasks.

source: Wang, Mao et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (AWM)
finding: LLM induces reusable workflows (sub-routines with abstracted example values) from past trajectories, offline or online, and puts them in memory. Improves web agents and cuts steps.
numbers: WebArena (GPT-4, temp 0): 35.5% total success vs 23.5% BrowserGym baseline = +12.0 points, +51.1% relative; steps reduced. Mind2Web cross-task step success +24.6% relative. Gap grows from 8.9 to 14.0 points as train-test distribution gap widens. Paper text gives 7.6% and 7.9% relative over SteP in different places.
limits: GPT-4 mostly; online mode learns from test tasks judged by an LLM evaluator, so noisy workflows can enter. Internal inconsistency in reported SteP margin.
agent_relevance: Strongest generalisation evidence for abstract routines (variables abstracted) over raw examples. Matches ACT-R: compiled rules generalise through variables.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners (AAAI)
finding: Agent writes natural-language insights from success/failure pairs (ADD/EDIT/REMOVE/AGREE operations) and retrieves similar past trajectories. Both parts are needed. Hand-crafted insights helped less than LLM-written ones; adding reflections into the insight step hurt.
numbers: HotpotQA, ALFWorld, WebShop vs ReAct/Act baselines (std err reported). Text: ExpeL matches Reflexion on HotpotQA (40% at R3 vs 39%) and beats it on ALFWorld (59% vs 54% at R3) without repeated attempts. Retrieve-only and insights-only both below full ExpeL. WebShop stays at the low end of Reflexion.
limits: Table layout was garbled in the text extraction; figures taken from prose. GPT-3.5/4 only. Insights are text lessons, not executable routines.
agent_relevance: Evidence on the lesson side of 'lesson to routine'. Insight quality needs an LLM writer and an edit loop; unverified reflection mixed in lowers quality.

source: Fang et al. (2025) Memp: Exploring Agent Procedural Memory
finding: Compares three forms of procedural memory: step-level script abstraction, full trajectory, and both combined ('proceduralization'). Combined form is best or tied in most cells. Memory also updated and deprecated over time.
numbers: GPT-4o, ALFWorld test success / steps: no memory 42.14% / 23.76; script 56.43%; trajectory 74.29%; proceduralization 77.86% / 15.01 steps. Dev: 39.28 -> 87.14 (proceduralization). TravelPlanner commonsense score 71.93 -> 79.94. Claude ALFWorld test: 53.59 script, 71.78 trajectory, 74.72 proceduralization.
limits: Two benchmarks. Scripts generalise better to the test set relative to the dev set; trajectories do better on tasks close to training ones. Table columns reconstructed from text extraction.
agent_relevance: The closest named test of compilation in LLMs: keeping both the abstract rule and a concrete example beats either alone, a lesson for how routines should be stored.

source: Memp: transfer across models
finding: Procedural memory built by a stronger model keeps its value when moved to a weaker model, and more refinement over time raises success and cuts steps on similar tasks.
numbers: Abstract states substantial gains after migration; exact weaker-model numbers not read in the pages opened.
limits: Numbers for migration not extracted. Gains are on analogous tasks within one benchmark family.
agent_relevance: Routines written by a strong model can be run by a cheap one, the same cost logic as LATM. Supports a build-once, run-cheap split.

source: Ouyang et al. (2025) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Distils strategy-level memory items from both successes and failures. Beats no-memory, Synapse (raw trajectories) and AWM (workflows only from successes). Adding test-time scaling (MaTTS) helps more.
numbers: WebArena overall success / steps, Gemini-2.5-flash: no memory 40.5 / 9.7; Synapse 42.1 / 9.2; AWM 44.1 / 9.0; ReasoningBank 48.8 / 8.3; +MaTTS 51.8 / 7.9. Gemini-2.5-pro: no memory 46.7 / 8.8; AWM 47.6 / 8.7. Paper claims up to 20% relative gain and 16% fewer steps.
limits: AWM gain over no memory on Gemini-2.5-pro is only +0.9; multi-site tasks fell for AWM (3.4 vs 10.3 no memory on flash). Gains depend on backbone.
agent_relevance: Learning from failures as well as successes matters. ACT-R compilation also stores error-driven rules (Taatgen 2002). AWM's success-only routines can hurt on mixed tasks.

source: Wang, Gandhi, Neubig & Fried (2025) Inducing Programmatic Skills for Agentic Tasks (ASI), COLM 2025
finding: Skills induced as executable programs and verified by re-running the trajectory with the skill (the last step must give the right answer) beat text-form workflows. Skills compose primitive actions into higher-level actions, reducing steps. This is composition, as in ACT-R.
numbers: WebArena: +23.5% over static baseline and +11.3% over text-skill AWM (success rate, relative as stated in abstract); steps cut by 10.7-15.3%. Claude table: vanilla 32.7% / 5.6 steps; AWM 36.3% / 5.9; ASI 40.4% / 5.0. Thought text cut from 87.9 to 13.4 tokens per step in induction data.
limits: Gains credited to programmatic verification. Skill transfer to new sites is partial: incompatible skills must be rewritten when sites change.
agent_relevance: Most direct match to 'merge steps into a faster rule with a check'. Verification before storing is the key part (G3). Fewer steps per task is the measurable proxy for compilation speedup.

source: Cai et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Tool Makers (LATM), ICLR 2024
finding: A strong model writes a reusable Python function from a few examples; a cheap model calls it on later instances. A dispatcher decides whether to reuse a cached tool. A 'functional cache'.
numbers: Accuracy CoT -> LATM with GPT-3.5 Turbo user: logical deduction 66.4 -> 79.7; tracking objects 61.6 -> 99.6; shuffled/sorting tasks 20.4 -> 92.2; Dyck 59.2 -> 98.3; remainder theorem 0.0 -> 100.0; schedule meeting 18.9 -> 100.0. GPT-4 CoT 88.8/100/63.6/90.9/0.0/55.6 vs GPT-4 LATM 86.6/100/87.5/99.1/100/100. GPT-4 call is over 15x the cost of a GPT-3.5 call.
limits: Big-Bench-Hard style tasks that are algorithmic; tool quality verified with validation examples. Logical deduction fell for GPT-4 (88.8 -> 86.6). Works where a single function covers a task class.
agent_relevance: Shows compiled routines can replace in-context reasoning for rule-like task classes and cut cost. Weak fit for fuzzy tasks. Cost split: pay once to compile, run cheap many times.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) SkillWeaver: Web Agents can Self-Improve by Discovering and Honing Skills
finding: Agent explores a site, proposes skills, practises them, and keeps those that pass tests, stored as Python APIs. Skills from a strong agent transfer to weaker ones.
numbers: Relative success gains: WebArena +31.8%, real-world sites (Online-Mind2Web tasks) +39.8%. 25% to 38% after 160 iterations of the pipeline. Weaker agents gain 40% to 130%. Transfer up to +54.3% on WebArena.
limits: Relative gains from low baselines. Depends on a reliable practise-and-verify step.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as Memp and LATM: strong-model compile, weak-model run. A test run before storing is the shared ingredient.

source: Jiang et al. (2026) SoK: Agentic Skills - Beyond Tool Use in LLM Agents
finding: Maps ACT-R's declarative/procedural split onto agents: skills are the procedural memory of an agent. Reviews skill learning systems from 2020 to early 2025 (Voyager, ReAct, Reflexion, SWE-agent as seeds) plus one 2026 benchmark, SkillsBench.
numbers: Taxonomy paper; no new experiments in the section read.
limits: Conceptual mapping; does not test ACT-R mechanisms such as utility-based selection or compile thresholds.
agent_relevance: Confirms nobody has tested production-compilation parameters (when to compile, how many co-firings) in LLM agents.

source: Chen et al. (2026) SkVM: Revisiting Language VM for Skills across Heterogeneous LLMs and Harnesses
finding: Treats skills as code and LLMs as processors. Finds that handing skills to models as raw context often does not help. Adds compile-time profiling and runtime 'JIT code solidification' that turns repeated skill steps into code.
numbers: Analysis of 118,000 skills (28,990 + 89,280 from two registries). Across 8 models, skills degrade performance on 15% of tasks (7% for Opus 4.6, 25% for Qwen3-30B); score unchanged on another 17%. SWE-bench-type study: 39 of 49 skills gave no gain, 3 clearly hurt. SkVM: up to 40% fewer tokens, up to 3.2x speedup by parallelism, 19-50x lower latency by code solidification.
limits: Latency gain is from replacing LLM calls with code on repeated steps, not accuracy gain. Skill benchmarks reported by others (SkillsBench) in the cited work.
agent_relevance: A failure case: text lessons given as skills can hurt weaker models. Solidifying a frequent step into code is a machine form of production compilation and gives the biggest latency drop.

source: Ellis et al. (2020/2021) DreamCoder: wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Wake phase solves tasks by search with the current library; sleep abstraction compresses found programs into new library routines; sleep dreaming trains a neural guide on replays and fantasies. Higher-level routines let problems be solved in fewer function calls, so search gets shallower.
numbers: Rediscovers list-processing basics, vector algebra and physics laws. In graphics and tower-building domains no alternative model solved over 60% of held-out tasks. Reports library learning decreases program depth while raising breadth.
limits: Needs a defined DSL and many search steps. Not an LLM system. Compression is Bayesian (shorter total description), not a firing-count threshold.
agent_relevance: The older AI parallel to compilation with a clear criterion: add a routine only if it shortens the combined programs. Gives a principled admission rule beside ACT-R's co-firing counts.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents (CodeAct)
finding: Letting the agent emit code as its action merges several tool calls into one action. Fewer interaction turns.
numbers: Up to 20% absolute higher success rate than text or JSON actions and up to 30% fewer actions. About 2.1 fewer turns on average in one comparison.
limits: Gain is from action format, not from learning or compiling over time.
agent_relevance: Shows the step-merging half of compilation (several actions in one) can work without learning. Compiled routines should be code-shaped for the same reason.

source: Authors (2024) LLM-ACTR: Cognitive LLMs for manufacturing decision-making
finding: Injects latent representations from an ACT-R model into LLM adapter layers and fine-tunes. Beats a Llama baseline at predicting human design choices, but it uses ACT-R traces, not production compilation.
numbers: Accuracy 0.6576, NLL 0.6534 (LLM-ACTR) vs chance 0.4826 / 0.6931 and LlaMa 0.3564 / 1.1330. Single-facet targets accuracy 0.64 (NLL 0.63); multi-facet 0.42 (NLL 1.18).
limits: Requires fine-tuning, so outside our no-training constraint. Single task domain. Does not model learning over time.
agent_relevance: Only LLM-with-ACT-R result found: model-based features help prediction of human choices, but accuracy falls on multi-factor choices. Not evidence for compilation.

source: Search finding (2020-2026 literature)
finding: No paper found that directly implements ACT-R production compilation (co-firing counts, utility, compile-then-specialise) in an LLM agent. Papers (Wray et al. 2025; SoK 2026) only cite the analogy. Practical systems (Voyager, AWM, ASI, LATM, SkillWeaver, SkVM) implement a looser form: verify, store, retrieve.
numbers: Searches: one web search plus citations traced in Wray et al. 2025 and the SoK 2026.
limits: Absence of evidence; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited, arXiv search returned nothing, so recall is incomplete.
agent_relevance: Our compile-threshold design (promote a lesson after N verified uses) is untested; it is a gap and a [D] item, not an established result.

source: Comparison of ACT-R vs LLM-agent compilation triggers (from c01, c05, c07, c12)
finding: ACT-R compiles after two rules fire in sequence (automatic, no verification). LLM systems compile after a verified success (Voyager, ASI), after an LLM judge says success (AWM online), or after a stronger-model write-up (LATM, SkillWeaver). The LLM versions all add a check that ACT-R lacks.
numbers: ASI: verified programmatic skills +11.3% over unverified text workflows (AWM) on WebArena.
limits: Synthesis across systems with different benchmarks, so numbers are not directly comparable.
agent_relevance: Supports a verified-compile rule: promote a lesson to a routine only after it passes a held-out check (G3).

source: AWM online vs test-time noise (Table 1 of AWM)
finding: Online AWM builds workflows from test tasks while it runs, with no human labels. It beat a method using 14 human-written workflows (SteP) despite no domain tuning.
numbers: AWM 35.5% vs SteP about 32-33% on WebArena (text reports 7.6% relative; abstract text says 7.9%). Baseline BrowserGym 23.5%.
limits: Margin over SteP is small and quoted inconsistently in the paper.
agent_relevance: Machine-induced routines can match hand-written ones; but verify the exact margin before citing.

source: ExpeL insight-extraction ablation (Table 3)
finding: Insight quality depends on the writer model and prompt. Hand-crafted insights gave a boost over ReAct but less than LLM-generated insights. Adding reflections into insight generation hurt.
numbers: HotpotQA SR roughly 28-32% for the weaker variants vs 39.0 +- 1.7 for full ExpeL; ALFWorld full ExpeL 59.0 +- 0.3 (mapping of rows to cells is approximate because the table text was garbled).
limits: Row-to-column mapping uncertain. Uses gpt-3.5 for execution and gpt-4 for insights.
agent_relevance: Lesson writing is a separate skill from task solving. Use the stronger model for compile and keep unverified self-reflection out of the routine.

source: Memp: script vs trajectory trade-off
finding: Scripts (abstract) generalise to new tasks; trajectories (concrete) win on tasks near the training ones. Combined is best. This is the same specialisation vs generality trade-off ACT-R shows when compiled rules are over-specific.
numbers: GPT-4o ALFWorld dev: script 66.67, trajectory 67.17, proceduralization 87.14; test: script 56.43, trajectory 74.29, proceduralization 77.86.
limits: Trajectory beats script on test here (74.29 vs 56.43) for GPT-4o, so the generalisation claim is not uniform across models.
agent_relevance: Store a routine plus one worked example; do not rely on the abstract form alone.

source: SkVM skill-use degradation (Section 1)
finding: Giving agents skills in context can reduce performance for some models, so a stored routine is not free. Smaller models are hurt more.
numbers: Degrades on 15% of tasks overall; 7% for Opus 4.6 and 25% for Qwen3-30B; up to 87% of tasks have at least one model with no gain; 451% token increase cited in one case.
limits: Reported in the introduction with citations to other studies; not independently re-run here.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: gate each routine's use with a trigger check and keep a fallback to plain reasoning. Measure routines on tasks they were not made from.

source: Voyager skill library: self-verification gate
finding: A program is committed to the library only after a critic module confirms the task is done in the environment. Retrieval uses the embedding of the skill description.
numbers: Skill library implemented as a vector database; see c05 and c06 for gains.
limits: Critic is another GPT-4 call, so correlated errors are possible (our G4).
agent_relevance: Use a code check as gate in place of a model critic where possible.

source: Taatgen & Lee (2003), declarative-first design
finding: Early performance is slow because instructions are held as facts and interpreted step by step. The authors attribute the model's advantage on trial 1 to it having all declarative knowledge, while people must still learn screen locations (Lee & Anderson 2001).
numbers: Model r2=.97 on overall landings; initial model advantage on trial 1.
limits: Explanation is the authors' reading, not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: For an LLM, 'declarative first' is free: the lesson text is in context from step one. The open question is what extra compilation adds once reading is cheap; only the cost and error rate can improve.
